summary: Shelburne Harbour's light on McNutt's Island, first lit in 1788, rebuilt after a 1959 lightning fire, automated in 1986 and reached only by boat today.

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property on McNutt's Island, reached only by boat. Grounds open, tower closed.

events.note: Lit from a stone octagonal tower on the southeast point of McNutt's Island
New keeper's house, built the year after the 1833 Commissioners' description
Worn-out lamps replaced: nine catoptric lamps in the lantern and three in a bow window, as an inspection report is quoted
Square fog-alarm building for a steam fog trumpet; the Society dates the fog signal to 1884
Third-order lens in a new lantern; upper light became flashing and the lower light was discontinued. The Society dates the third-order dioptric lens to 1922.
Good Luck ran aground in a blizzard on the night of 2 January 1937 and sank; crew reached shore
Lightning struck the stone tower and the fire severely damaged it
Temporary light set on the roof of the fog alarm building while the old tower was demolished
Octagonal concrete tower replaces the burned stone tower; Cameron Contracting Ltd. paid $24,382 to build it
Automated; station unmanned, houses vacant from 1986
Electric lantern; flashing white every 10 seconds

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends and the Archives give 1788 for the light; the Society's list gives 'Began: 1787' and 'Year Lit: 1788'. The story uses 1788 for the light and 1787 only as the start of the work.
Lighthouse Friends dates the square fog-alarm building to 1883; the Society dates the fog signal to 1884. Both are reported in the story as the building and the signal.

The Society's detail table gives a temporary light in 1959 and the replacement tower in 1961; its heritage text places a temporary light on the fog-alarm roof in 1960 while the old tower came down. Read together: the old tower burned in 1959, was demolished about 1960, and the concrete tower was lit in 1961.

notes_for_editor: Sources are secondary for most of the story: Lighthouse Friends and the Society each give a narrative and a keeper roster, and they disagree. (1) Keeper roster: Lighthouse Friends has Otis Orchard as assistant from 1921 and head keeper 1944-1953 and Beaumont Decker head keeper 1920-1944; the Society has Orchard head keeper 1920-1956 and no Decker. Not resolved; the story gives both. (2) The Lighthouse Friends narrative says the first keeper died in 1821, its roster and the Yarbrough blog say 1812, and the Society's roster says 'Cockeren, Capt. Alexander 1788-1857'. Not resolved. (3) Bernice Goodick's father was keeper until June 1956 (Society). His name is not given in any source read, so he is not on the roster; a named keeper would need a source. (4) Lens year: 1919 (Lighthouse Friends) against 1922 (Society). (5) Structure height: the Coast Guard list gives 17.3 m; the Society gives 48 ft (about 14.6 m); the story gives both. (6) The Society's essay gives the 1788 tower as '92-foot' but its detail table gives 77 ft; the story uses 23.5 m, which Lighthouse Friends and the Society's table agree on. (7) Second-hand: the 1833 and 1857 reports are read only as Lighthouse Friends quotes them; the 1950 Standard feature only as the Society quotes it; the 1860 letter only as the Yarbrough blog describes it (the Archives' RG 7 Vol. 43 was not consulted); Yarbrough's 2013 book was not read. (8) Corpus: the two Marine Department footnotes are the fog-alarm lines headed 'Cape Roseway', not matched by column position. The Marine report lines for 1900 and 1909 are not shared with any other station. (9) Not searched: Chronicling America (US papers, not Canadian stations). The 1950 feature gives the range as '18 miles' with no unit; the story uses the Coast Guard's 10 nautical miles. (10) Sambro's date differs (1758 in the Archives and the Society; 1760 in Lighthouse Friends); the story does not give it. (11) Corrections: none proposed. The station record's first_lit (1788), status and position agree with the Coast Guard list. (12) Photos: none added. (13) Access: boat only; the Coast Guard tower is closed; the story says so in Today.
